title: Multimodal, local models & fine-tuning hands-on
scopeHtml: Scope: Sending images, PDFs and audio to models, running local models (Ollama, llama.cpp, transformers), quantization, choosing prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning, LoRA/QLoRA, evaluating a tuned model, licensing and data privacy.

notes.title: What multimodal means and how images become tokens
notes.html:
The simple idea. A normal LLM (large language model) reads and writes text only. A multimodal model also accepts other kinds of input, called modalities: images, PDFs (pages are rendered as images plus extracted text), sometimes audio and video. Output is usually still text. Some models also produce images or speech, but for backend work "image/PDF in, text out" is the 90 percent case.

Key terms first.

  • Token: a small chunk of text (roughly 3 to 4 English characters) that the model counts and bills in. Everything the model sees is turned into tokens.
  • Prompt: everything you send to the model (instructions, question, attachments).
  • Context window: the maximum number of tokens (input plus output) the model can handle in one request.
  • Vision encoder: a small neural network bolted onto the LLM that turns an image into a list of vectors ("image tokens") the LLM can read like words.

How an image becomes tokens (mechanism). The image is resized so it fits a size limit, cut into a grid of small patches (for example 14 by 14 pixels), each patch is turned into a vector by the vision encoder, and those vectors are fed to the LLM next to your text tokens. So an image costs tokens, and a bigger image costs more. Anthropic documents an approximate rule of about width times height divided by 750 tokens, with large images being downscaled first (verify the exact numbers and size limits in the current docs). Other vendors use tiles of fixed size with a fixed cost per tile.

 photo.jpg ---> resize ---> cut into patches ---> vision encoder ---> image tokens --+
                                                                                     +--> LLM --> text answer
 "What is wrong with this wiring?" ---> tokenizer ---> text tokens ------------------+

Why this matters in practice.

  • Cost and latency grow with image size, so send the smallest image that still shows the detail you need.
  • The model "sees" patches, not pixels: tiny text, thin lines and dense tables can be misread.
  • The model can hallucinate (confidently invent) details that are not in the image.

Real-world examples. Google Lens and Gemini in Google Photos answer questions about pictures. Be My Eyes uses a vision model to describe surroundings for blind users. Insurance apps let you photograph car damage and get a first estimate. Expense apps such as Expensify read receipts. Claude, GPT and Gemini all accept images through their APIs.

Analogy (after the explanation). Think of a translator who only speaks text. The vision encoder is a sketch artist who describes the photo in the translator's own language (vectors). The more detailed the sketch (bigger image), the longer the briefing takes and the more it costs.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the LLM "looks at pixels directly". It reads encoder outputs (image tokens), and those count toward the context window and the bill.
  • Forgetting that images consume tokens and can push a long conversation past the context window.
  • Assuming a vision model is a reliable OCR or measuring tool. It can misread small text and invent details; validate important fields.
  • Mixing up modalities: most text LLM APIs accept image input but not every API accepts audio input directly (see the audio section).

notes.title: Sending images to a model with code
notes.html:
The simple idea. You send the image inside the message as a content block next to the text block. There are two ways to attach it: as base64 (the image bytes encoded as text, works anywhere) or as a URL (the provider downloads it; the URL must be publicly reachable).

Mechanism with the Anthropic API. A user message holds a list of blocks. An image block has a source with type (base64 or url), and for base64 also media_type (image/jpeg, image/png, image/gif, image/webp) and data. Put the image before the question for best results. Keys come from the environment variable ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, never hard-coded.

# pip install anthropic   (reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment)
import base64, anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
with open("receipt.jpg", "rb") as f:
    img_b64 = base64.standard_b64encode(f.read()).decode()

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",          # verify current model ids in the docs
    max_tokens=500,
    messages=[{
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image",
             "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "image/jpeg", "data": img_b64}},
            {"type": "text", "text": "Extract merchant, date and total as JSON."},
        ],
    }],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)  # prints e.g. {"merchant": "Cafe X", "date": "2026-03-01", "total": 12.4}

For Kotlin and Java the most portable option is the plain REST call, because it does not depend on SDK builder names. (The official Java SDK com.anthropic:anthropic-java also supports image blocks; verify the exact builder methods in its docs.) Both snippets below send the same JSON.

// Kotlin (JVM) using only the JDK HttpClient; Android must call YOUR backend instead, never ship the key.
import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.*
import java.nio.file.*
import java.util.Base64

fun main() {
    val b64 = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(Files.readAllBytes(Path.of("receipt.jpg")))
    val body = """
      {"model":"claude-sonnet-5-5","max_tokens":500,
       "messages":[{"role":"user","content":[
         {"type":"image","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"image/jpeg","data":"$b64"}},
         {"type":"text","text":"Extract merchant, date and total as JSON."}]}]}
    """.trimIndent()
    val req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"))
        .header("x-api-key", System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
        .header("anthropic-version", "2023-06-01")
        .header("content-type", "application/json")
        .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
    val res = HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
    println(res.body()) // prints the JSON response; the answer is in content[0].text
}
// Java 17: same request with the JDK HttpClient (parse the JSON with Jackson in real code).
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.Base64;

public class ImageDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String b64 = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(Files.readAllBytes(Path.of("receipt.jpg")));
        String body = """
          {"model":"claude-sonnet-5-5","max_tokens":500,
           "messages":[{"role":"user","content":[
             {"type":"image","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"image/jpeg","data":"%s"}},
             {"type":"text","text":"Extract merchant, date and total as JSON."}]}]}
          """.formatted(b64);
        HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"))
            .header("x-api-key", System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
            .header("anthropic-version", "2023-06-01")
            .header("content-type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
        HttpResponse<String> res = HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        System.out.println(res.body()); // prints the JSON response; answer is in content[0].text
    }
}

Android specifics. The app should compress the photo (for example to a maximum 1568 px long edge, JPEG quality 80, a size worth verifying in provider docs), upload it to your own backend, and let the backend call the model. This keeps the API key off the phone and lets you add rate limits and logging. On-device alternatives are Gemini Nano via ML Kit GenAI and MediaPipe LLM Inference, which also support small image-capable models on some devices.

Real-world examples. Receipt scanners, ID-card field extraction, and "photo of a product, write the listing" tools in e-commerce all use this pattern. Many apps accept a gallery photo, resize on-device, then call a backend endpoint such as POST /describe.

Analogy. Base64 is mailing the photo inside the envelope; a URL is writing the address where the recipient can go and fetch the photo themselves. If the address is private, they cannot fetch it.

Common interview traps.

  • Sending very large images as base64 and hitting the request size limit; resize first.
  • Using a URL that requires a login or is on localhost; the provider cannot fetch it.
  • Putting the API key inside the Android APK.
  • Wrong media_type (says jpeg, bytes are png) causing an error or garbled result.

notes.title: PDFs and audio
notes.html:
PDFs, the simple idea. A PDF is a document of pages. Modern APIs let you attach it directly as a document block. The provider extracts the text and also renders each page as an image, so the model can read charts, tables and scanned pages. This replaces a lot of old OCR (optical character recognition) plumbing.

Mechanism. In the Anthropic API the block is {"type":"document","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"application/pdf","data":...}}. Each page costs text tokens plus image tokens, so a 100-page PDF is expensive and may exceed page and size limits (verify the current limits). For large files, or files you will ask many questions about, use a Files API where available, prompt caching (reuse the same prefix cheaply on later calls) or RAG (retrieval-augmented generation: search the document first and send only the relevant pieces).

# Ask a question about a PDF (document block, same message shape as the image example).
import base64, anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
pdf = base64.standard_b64encode(open("contract.pdf", "rb").read()).decode()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=600,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "document", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": pdf}},
        {"type": "text", "text": "List the termination clauses with page numbers."},
    ]}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)  # prints a bulleted list of clauses
// Kotlin: only the content blocks change versus the image example; the HTTP call is identical.
val pdfB64 = java.util.Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(java.nio.file.Files.readAllBytes(java.nio.file.Path.of("contract.pdf")))
val contentJson = """
  [{"type":"document","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"application/pdf","data":"$pdfB64"}},
   {"type":"text","text":"List the termination clauses with page numbers."}]
"""
// put contentJson in messages[0].content and POST to /v1/messages as shown earlier
// Java: same swap, only the content array differs.
String pdfB64 = java.util.Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(java.nio.file.Files.readAllBytes(java.nio.file.Path.of("contract.pdf")));
String contentJson = """
  [{"type":"document","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"application/pdf","data":"%s"}},
   {"type":"text","text":"List the termination clauses with page numbers."}]
  """.formatted(pdfB64);
// put contentJson in messages[0].content and POST to /v1/messages as shown earlier

Audio, the simple idea. Audio is different. Several providers (Gemini, GPT audio models) accept audio input directly, but the Claude API at the time of writing takes text, images and PDFs, not raw audio (verify current docs). The classic, provider-neutral pipeline is speech to text, then LLM, then optionally text to speech.

 mic/recording --> ASR (Whisper, Deepgram, Android SpeechRecognizer) --> text --> LLM --> text --> TTS (optional)

ASR means automatic speech recognition. Whisper is an open-source ASR model from OpenAI that you can run locally. Practical points: split long recordings into chunks (for example 30 seconds to a few minutes), keep timestamps if you need citations, and remember that speaker labels (diarization) need an extra step.

# pip install openai-whisper  (local, free; downloads the model on first use)
import whisper
model = whisper.load_model("base")
text = model.transcribe("meeting.mp3")["text"]
print(text[:200])  # prints the first 200 characters of the transcript, then send `text` to the LLM
// Kotlin/Android: use the platform recognizer or call your backend; verify API details in Android docs.
// Android: SpeechRecognizer.createSpeechRecognizer(context) streams partial text results.
// JVM backend: upload the audio file to your Python Whisper service with a multipart POST, get {"text": "..."} back.
// Java: there is no first-party Whisper binding in the JDK; the common approach is a small HTTP service.
// POST the audio to a Python Whisper service (or a hosted transcription API) and read the text field from the JSON.
// Then pass that text to the LLM exactly like any other prompt.

Real-world examples. Zoom and Google Meet summaries transcribe first, then summarize. Otter.ai and Fireflies do meeting notes. Voice assistants chain ASR, LLM and TTS (some now use single end-to-end speech models for lower latency). Call-center QA tools transcribe calls and score them with an LLM.

Analogy. A PDF with a document block is handing a clerk the whole folder; RAG is giving them the index and asking them to pull out only the three relevant pages. Audio via ASR is hiring a stenographer first, then handing the typed transcript to the analyst.

Common interview traps.

  • Sending a 300-page PDF on every request instead of using RAG or prompt caching; the cost explodes.
  • Claiming every model accepts audio. Many do not; transcribe first.
  • Ignoring that scanned PDFs have no text layer; direct page-image reading helps but accuracy still needs checking.
  • Forgetting privacy: audio and documents often contain personal data (see the privacy section).

notes.title: Vision use cases and what goes wrong in production
notes.html:
The simple idea. Vision models are best for tasks where structure is messy: forms, receipts, screenshots, charts, diagrams, handwriting, product photos.

Common use cases.

  • Document extraction: invoice or receipt to JSON (merchant, date, total, line items).
  • UI understanding: a screenshot to bug description or test steps; also used by "computer use" agents that click on screens.
  • Chart and table reading: pull numbers from a bar chart image.
  • Visual QA and moderation: "does this photo contain a damaged package?", unsafe image checks.
  • Accessibility: automatic alt text, scene description.

Mechanism for reliable extraction. Ask for strict JSON, give the schema in the prompt (or use the provider's structured output / tool calling so the output must match a schema), tell the model to answer null when a field is not visible, and validate the result in code.

import json
prompt = ('Return ONLY JSON: {"merchant": str|null, "date": "YYYY-MM-DD"|null, "total": number|null}. '
          'Use null if not clearly visible. Do not guess.')
data = json.loads(msg.content[0].text)   # msg is the response from the image example
assert data["total"] is None or isinstance(data["total"], (int, float))  # validate before saving
print(data)  # prints {'merchant': 'Cafe X', 'date': '2026-03-01', 'total': 12.4}
// Kotlin with kotlinx.serialization: a data class is your schema and your validator.
@kotlinx.serialization.Serializable
data class Receipt(val merchant: String? = null, val date: String? = null, val total: Double? = null)

val r = kotlinx.serialization.json.Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }
    .decodeFromString<Receipt>(modelText)   // throws on malformed JSON: catch it and retry or flag for review
println(r) // prints Receipt(merchant=Cafe X, date=2026-03-01, total=12.4)
// Java 17 record + Jackson: malformed or mistyped JSON throws, which is exactly what you want.
record Receipt(String merchant, String date, Double total) {}
ObjectMapper om = new ObjectMapper().configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false);
Receipt r = om.readValue(modelText, Receipt.class);
System.out.println(r); // prints Receipt[merchant=Cafe X, date=2026-03-01, total=12.4]

What goes wrong in production.

  • Hallucinated fields (a total that is not on the receipt). Fix: null-if-unsure instruction, cross-check (line items sum to total), human review queue for low-confidence cases.
  • Resolution loss: a phone photo downscaled too hard. Fix: crop to the region of interest, or tile the image.
  • Rotation and glare: pre-process (auto-rotate, crop).
  • Cost drift: five images per request at high resolution multiplies the bill. Track tokens per request.
  • Prompt injection through images: text inside an image (for example "ignore previous instructions") can steer the model. Treat image content as untrusted data.
  • Bias and safety: models may refuse or be unreliable at identifying people from faces; do not build identity features on them.

Real-world examples. Banks' check deposit and expense apps (Expensify, Ramp) extract fields and route low-confidence ones to humans. Customer-support tools read screenshots users attach to tickets. Retail apps compare shelf photos to planograms.

Analogy. Using a vision model for extraction is like a quick but sometimes overconfident intern: very fast, good with messy forms, but a supervisor (your validation code) must check the numbers.

Common interview traps.

  • Trusting the model's JSON without schema validation.
  • Not giving a "not visible" escape hatch, which pushes the model to guess.
  • Treating text in images as trusted instructions (prompt injection).
  • Comparing cost only by per-token price and forgetting image token counts.

notes.title: Why run models locally and how Ollama works
notes.html:
The simple idea. A local model runs on your own machine or server instead of a vendor's cloud API. The model is just a big file of numbers (weights); a program loads it into RAM or GPU memory (VRAM) and computes answers.

Why people do it.

  • Privacy: data never leaves your network (health, legal, source code).
  • Cost at volume: no per-token bill; you pay for hardware.
  • Offline use and predictable latency (no network).
  • Control: pin a version, fine-tune, no surprise deprecations.
  • Trade-off: open models you can run on a laptop are usually smaller and weaker than frontier cloud models, and you now own operations (updates, scaling, monitoring).

Ollama. Ollama is a free tool that downloads models and runs them behind a local HTTP server (default http://localhost:11434). You do not manage files or GPU code yourself. It builds on llama.cpp under the hood and handles quantized models in GGUF format.

 your app --HTTP--> Ollama server (localhost:11434) --> loads model (GGUF) into RAM/VRAM --> tokens back

Commands (model names change often; check the Ollama library):

ollama pull llama3.2         # download a small model
ollama run llama3.2          # chat in the terminal
ollama list                  # show downloaded models

Ollama exposes its own /api/chat endpoint and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint at /v1, so code written for the OpenAI client often works by changing only the base URL.

# pip install ollama      (talks to the local server; `ollama pull llama3.2` first)
import ollama
r = ollama.chat(model="llama3.2", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain quantization in one line."}])
print(r["message"]["content"])  # prints the model's one-line answer
# Vision: use a vision-capable model and add "images": ["photo.jpg"] to the message.
// Kotlin: plain HTTP to the local server (no key needed). stream=false returns one JSON object.
val body = """{"model":"llama3.2","stream":false,
  "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain quantization in one line."}]}"""
val req = java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder(java.net.URI("http://localhost:11434/api/chat"))
    .POST(java.net.http.HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
println(java.net.http.HttpClient.newHttpClient()
    .send(req, java.net.http.HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body()) // prints JSON with message.content
// Java 17: same call with LangChain4j would also work (langchain4j-ollama); shown here as raw HTTP.
String body = """
  {"model":"llama3.2","stream":false,
   "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain quantization in one line."}]}
  """;
HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://localhost:11434/api/chat"))
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
System.out.println(HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());
// prints JSON; the answer is at message.content

Spring AI and LangChain4j both have Ollama starters, so a Spring Boot service can swap between a cloud model and a local one by configuration (verify the current property names in their docs).

Real-world examples. Developers run local code assistants (Continue, Cline with Ollama) so proprietary code stays private. Hospitals and law firms pilot on-prem models. Teams use Ollama in CI and for local development to avoid cloud bills, then switch to a hosted model in production.

Analogy. Cloud API is eating at a restaurant (no kitchen to maintain, but you pay per meal and share your order with them). A local model is cooking at home: private and cheaper per meal at scale, but you buy the stove and clean up.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying local is always cheaper. Idle GPUs, engineers' time and low utilization make it more expensive at low volume.
  • Exposing Ollama's port to the internet; it has no authentication by default.
  • Forgetting the context window setting: local runtimes often default to a small context and silently truncate long prompts (set it explicitly, verify the option name).
  • Expecting a laptop-sized model to match frontier quality on hard reasoning.

notes.title: llama.cpp and Hugging Face transformers
notes.html:
The simple idea. Ollama is the friendly wrapper. Underneath and beside it are two main engines: llama.cpp (C/C++, fast on CPUs and consumer GPUs, uses GGUF model files) and Hugging Face transformers (Python library, uses PyTorch, the standard for research, training and the biggest model hub).

Hugging Face basics. The Hub is a website hosting models, datasets and demos. transformers downloads a model by name, with a tokenizer (the code that converts text to token ids and back). Format on the Hub is usually safetensors (a safe weight file; avoid pickle-based files from unknown sources because pickle can execute code on load).

# pip install transformers accelerate torch   (model id is an example; check the license and gating on the Hub)
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name, device_map="auto")
inputs = tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": "Say hi in French."}],
                                 add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
out = model.generate(inputs, max_new_tokens=30)
print(tok.decode(out[0][inputs.shape[-1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))  # prints "Bonjour !" or similar

llama.cpp as a server. It ships llama-server, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API, so any backend can call it.

llama-server -m ./model-Q4_K_M.gguf -c 4096 --port 8080     # -c is the context size in tokens
# then POST http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions
# Python: the standard OpenAI client pointed at llama-server (or Ollama's /v1)
from openai import OpenAI
c = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8080/v1", api_key="not-needed")
r = c.chat.completions.create(model="local", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}])
print(r.choices[0].message.content)  # prints the reply from the local model
// Kotlin: reuse the same HTTP pattern; only the URL and body shape change (OpenAI format).
val body = """{"model":"local","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hi"}]}"""
val req = java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder(java.net.URI("http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions"))
    .header("content-type", "application/json")
    .POST(java.net.http.HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
// response JSON: choices[0].message.content
// Java: LangChain4j can target any OpenAI-compatible server by base URL (verify builder names in its docs):
// OpenAiChatModel.builder().baseUrl("http://localhost:8080/v1").apiKey("not-needed").modelName("local").build()
// Or reuse the HttpClient pattern from the Ollama section with this URL and body.

Which to choose. transformers for experiments, fine-tuning and models not yet converted; Ollama for quick local dev; llama.cpp for lean deployment or edge devices; for high-throughput GPU serving in production use a dedicated server such as vLLM (continuous batching, PagedAttention). On Android, llama.cpp-based apps and MediaPipe LLM Inference run small models on-device.

Real-world examples. LM Studio and Jan wrap llama.cpp in desktop apps. Hugging Face powers most open-model releases (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma families). Many privacy-focused mobile apps embed llama.cpp.

Analogy. Hugging Face is the giant library with the original manuscripts and the printing press; llama.cpp is a pocket paperback edition that fits in your bag; Ollama is a vending machine that hands you the pocket edition with one button.

Common interview traps.

  • Loading unknown pickle (.bin/.pt) checkpoints, which can execute malicious code; prefer safetensors.
  • Forgetting the chat template; feeding raw text to an instruct model gives poor results.
  • Using transformers directly for high-concurrency production serving instead of a batching server.
  • Thinking GGUF can be used for training; it is an inference format.

notes.title: Quantization in practice
notes.html:
The simple idea. Model weights are numbers. Stored as 16-bit floats, an 8-billion-parameter model needs about 16 GB. Quantization stores each number with fewer bits (8, 4 or even less), shrinking memory and often speeding up inference, at a small cost in quality.

Mechanism. Weights are grouped in blocks; each block stores a scale (and sometimes a zero-point) plus low-bit integers. At compute time they are converted back approximately. The error is small because weights cluster near zero and blocks adapt their scale.

Memory arithmetic (rule of thumb). Memory is roughly parameters times bits divided by 8, plus overhead for the KV cache and runtime.

Model fp16 (16-bit) 8-bit 4-bit
8B params ~16 GB ~8 GB ~4.5 to 5 GB
70B params ~140 GB ~70 GB ~40 GB

Add a few extra GB for the KV cache (the stored attention keys/values for the tokens so far, which grows with context length).

Formats you will meet.

  • GGUF with names like Q8_0, Q5_K_M, Q4_K_M: llama.cpp/Ollama. Q4_K_M is a popular balance. Lower numbers mean smaller and lossier.
  • GPTQ / AWQ: GPU-oriented 4-bit post-training quantization used with vLLM and transformers.
  • bitsandbytes (load_in_4bit, NF4): load a model in 4-bit inside transformers, central to QLoRA.
# Load a model in 4-bit with transformers + bitsandbytes (needs an NVIDIA GPU; verify package versions)
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig
cfg = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct", quantization_config=cfg, device_map="auto")
print(f"{model.get_memory_footprint()/1e9:.2f} GB")  # prints the in-memory size, a fraction of fp16
// Kotlin: quantization is done by tooling, your code only picks a model tag. With Ollama the tag selects it:
val model = "llama3.2:3b-instruct-q4_K_M"   // example tag; check the Ollama library for real tag names
// ...then call /api/chat with "model": model exactly as before.
// Java: same idea; quantization level is part of the model name you pass to the server.
String model = "llama3.2:3b-instruct-q4_K_M";   // example tag; verify in the Ollama library
// ...then call /api/chat or LangChain4j OllamaChatModel.builder().modelName(model) (verify builder in docs).

Converting yourself with llama.cpp (script names evolve; check the repo README):

python convert_hf_to_gguf.py ./my-hf-model --outfile model-f16.gguf
llama-quantize model-f16.gguf model-Q4_K_M.gguf Q4_K_M

Trade-offs. 8-bit is nearly lossless; 4-bit loses a little (noticeable on math, code and non-English); 2-3 bit loses more. Smaller models suffer more from quantization than big ones. Always test on your own task: compare the quantized and original on your evaluation set. Quantization speeds decoding mostly because decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound (fewer bytes to read per token).

Real-world examples. Nearly every model you pull with Ollama is a 4-bit GGUF. Phones run 4-bit small models (Gemma, Llama 3.2 1B/3B class) because RAM is limited. Hosted providers also serve quantized (fp8) models to cut cost.

Analogy. Quantization is saving a photo as a smaller JPEG: the file shrinks a lot, you rarely notice at normal quality, but compress too much and artifacts appear.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the KV cache and runtime overhead when sizing GPU memory.
  • Saying quantization is the same as pruning or distillation (those remove weights or train a smaller model).
  • Assuming a quantized model can be fine-tuned like normal; you train adapters on top (QLoRA), not the 4-bit weights directly.
  • Judging quality by perplexity alone instead of your own task metrics.

notes.title: Fine-tuning vs prompting vs RAG
notes.html:
The simple idea. Three ways to make a model do what you want. Try them in this order: prompting, then RAG, then fine-tuning.

  • Prompting: write better instructions, add examples (few-shot), request a format. Zero training, instant, cheap to iterate.
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): fetch relevant facts from your documents at question time and paste them into the prompt. Fixes missing or changing knowledge.
  • Fine-tuning: continue training the model on your examples so its behavior changes (tone, format, domain style, a narrow skill). It does not reliably add new facts and the knowledge is frozen at training time.
Is the problem missing/changing facts?        --> RAG
Is the problem style, format, a narrow skill, --> fine-tune (after prompting + few-shot fails or costs too much)
  or cost/latency of long prompts?
Is the problem unclear instructions?          --> prompt engineering first
Prompting RAG Fine-tuning
Fixes instructions, format stale or private knowledge style, format, narrow skill
Setup time minutes days days to weeks (data + eval)
Updating facts edit prompt re-index documents retrain
Citations no yes, possible no
Cost per-call tokens retrieval infra + tokens training + hosting

When fine-tuning is really worth it.

  • A strict output style the prompt cannot enforce reliably.
  • A small cheap model must match a big model's quality on one narrow task (distillation by fine-tuning: generate labeled data with the big model, train the small one).
  • Very long, repetitive prompts you want to remove to cut latency and cost.
  • Data cannot go to a third-party API, so you tune an open model locally.

When it is a bad idea. You have fewer than a few hundred good examples, the knowledge changes weekly, you cannot measure quality, or you have not tried better prompts. Fine-tuning on bad data produces a confidently wrong model.

Types. SFT (supervised fine-tuning on prompt/answer pairs), preference tuning (DPO and similar, teaching "this answer is better than that one"), and full fine-tuning versus parameter-efficient methods like LoRA (next section). Hosted vendors offer managed fine-tuning for some models (availability varies, verify per vendor and model).

# Decision helper as code: a tiny router many teams write mentally. Prints the first thing to try.
def first_try(needs_fresh_facts, needs_style_or_format, prompt_already_tuned):
    if needs_fresh_facts:
        return "RAG"
    if needs_style_or_format and prompt_already_tuned:
        return "fine-tune"
    return "prompting"
print(first_try(False, True, True))  # prints fine-tune
fun firstTry(freshFacts: Boolean, styleOrFormat: Boolean, promptTuned: Boolean) = when {
    freshFacts -> "RAG"
    styleOrFormat && promptTuned -> "fine-tune"
    else -> "prompting"
}
fun main() = println(firstTry(false, true, true)) // prints fine-tune
static String firstTry(boolean freshFacts, boolean styleOrFormat, boolean promptTuned) {
    if (freshFacts) return "RAG";
    if (styleOrFormat && promptTuned) return "fine-tune";
    return "prompting";
}
// System.out.println(firstTry(false, true, true)); // prints fine-tune

Real-world examples. Customer-support bots at companies typically use RAG over help-center articles, not fine-tuning, so updates are instant. GitHub Copilot-style code models are fine-tuned on code for behavior. Banks fine-tune small models to classify transactions or emails cheaply at scale. Many "brand voice" writers fine-tune on a few thousand approved texts.

Analogy. Prompting is giving a new employee written instructions; RAG is letting them look things up in the company wiki while working; fine-tuning is sending them to months of training so the habit becomes second nature, and the training does not update when the wiki does.

Common interview traps.

  • "Fine-tune the model on our documents so it knows them." That is usually a RAG job; tuned knowledge is unreliable and goes stale.
  • Skipping a baseline: never fine-tune before measuring the prompted model on the same test set.
  • Believing fine-tuning removes the need for guardrails or evaluation.
  • Ignoring maintenance: every base-model upgrade means re-tuning and re-evaluating.

notes.title: LoRA basics and training code (Python only)
notes.html:
The simple idea. Full fine-tuning updates all billions of weights, needing huge GPU memory. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the original weights and trains tiny extra matrices ("adapters") added to certain layers. Instead of changing a big matrix W (say 4096 by 4096, 16.7M numbers), you learn two small matrices A (4096 by r) and B (r by 4096) with a small rank r like 8 or 16, and use W + (alpha/r) times B times A. For r=16 that is about 131k trainable numbers instead of 16.7M for that matrix, often under 1 percent of the model overall. The adapter file is just tens to hundreds of MB.

QLoRA loads the frozen base model in 4-bit (from the quantization section) and trains LoRA adapters on top, letting you tune a 7-8B model on a single consumer or free-tier GPU.

Language note. Training code is Python only: the tooling (PyTorch, Hugging Face peft, trl) lives there. Kotlin and Java do not train models; they call the resulting model over HTTP, shown after the Python code.

 your examples (JSONL) --> tokenizer --> SFTTrainer (base frozen + LoRA adapters trained) --> adapter files
 adapter + base --> merge (optional) --> convert to GGUF --> Ollama / llama.cpp / vLLM --> your Kotlin/Java app calls it

Data format. A JSONL file with one example per line, in chat form:

{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Classify: 'card declined twice'"},{"role":"assistant","content":"payments_issue"}]}

Quality beats quantity: a few hundred to a few thousand clean, consistent, diverse examples often beat tens of thousands of noisy ones.

# pip install transformers peft trl datasets bitsandbytes accelerate    (APIs evolve: verify trl/peft docs for your versions)
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, BitsAndBytesConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

base = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"                       # small model so it trains on modest hardware
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(base)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    base, device_map="auto",
    quantization_config=BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
                                           bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16))  # QLoRA: frozen 4-bit base

lora = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
                  target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"],  # attention projections; names vary by model
                  task_type="CAUSAL_LM")

data = load_dataset("json", data_files={"train": "train.jsonl", "validation": "val.jsonl"})
trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model, train_dataset=data["train"], eval_dataset=data["validation"],
    peft_config=lora, processing_class=tok,
    args=SFTConfig(output_dir="out", num_train_epochs=2, per_device_train_batch_size=4,
                   learning_rate=2e-4, logging_steps=10, eval_strategy="epoch"))
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("out/adapter")   # prints loss lines while training; saves only the small adapter

Merging and serving. Either keep the adapter separate or merge it into the base:

from peft import PeftModel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
base_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct")
merged = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, "out/adapter").merge_and_unload()
merged.save_pretrained("out/merged")   # a normal HF model folder; convert to GGUF with llama.cpp, then `ollama create`
# Ollama can load the converted result with a Modelfile:
FROM ./merged-Q4_K_M.gguf
# (Ollama's Modelfile also supports an ADAPTER instruction for LoRA adapters; verify the supported base models in its docs.)
ollama create ticket-classifier -f Modelfile

Calling the tuned model from Kotlin and Java. To the caller it is just another model name on the server.

// Kotlin: identical to the earlier Ollama call, only the model name changes.
val body = """{"model":"ticket-classifier","stream":false,
  "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Classify: 'card declined twice'"}]}"""
// POST to http://localhost:11434/api/chat ; expect message.content == "payments_issue"
// Java: same HttpClient pattern; the tuned model is addressed by name.
String body = """
  {"model":"ticket-classifier","stream":false,
   "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Classify: 'card declined twice'"}]}
  """;
// POST to http://localhost:11434/api/chat ; expect message.content to be "payments_issue"

Key hyperparameters. Rank r (capacity: 8 to 64 typical), alpha (scaling, commonly 2 times r), target modules (more modules = more capacity and memory), learning rate (LoRA tolerates higher, around 1e-4 to 2e-4), epochs (1 to 3; more risks overfitting), batch size.

What goes wrong. Overfitting (train loss falls, validation worsens, the model parrots examples), catastrophic forgetting (it gets worse at general tasks), wrong chat template (the model ignores instructions), bad labels, out-of-memory errors (lower batch size, use gradient accumulation, shorter max length, QLoRA).

Real-world examples. Hugging Face PEFT, Unsloth, Axolotl and Torchtune are the widely used toolchains. Companies keep one base model and swap many small LoRA adapters per customer or task (multi-LoRA serving in vLLM and similar servers), which is far cheaper than hosting many full models.

Analogy. The base model is a printed textbook you are not allowed to write in. LoRA is a set of sticky notes added to certain pages: cheap, swappable, removable, and the original book stays untouched.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying LoRA trains all weights, or that it only works for text models; it freezes the base and trains low-rank adapters (also used for image models).
  • Training on prompts plus answers without checking that only assistant tokens are scored, or without using the right chat template.
  • Evaluating on training data and celebrating a low loss.
  • Believing Kotlin or Java are viable for training here; the practical answer is Python to train, any language to call.

notes.title: Evaluating a tuned model
notes.html:
The simple idea. "It seems better" is not a result. Evaluation means testing the model on examples it never trained on and scoring them, comparing against a baseline (the original model with a good prompt) so you know the fine-tune was worth it.

Step by step.

  1. Split the data before training: train / validation / test. The test set is locked until the end.
  2. Define metrics that match the task: accuracy or F1 for classification; exact match or JSON-schema validity for extraction; for free text, rubric scoring by humans or an LLM-as-judge (a strong model grades answers against criteria; calibrate it against human labels and watch for bias toward longer answers).
  3. Baselines: base model plus prompt, base model plus few-shot, and a bigger hosted model. If the tuned small model is not better on your metric, do not ship it.
  4. Regression checks for general ability and safety: run a small general benchmark or your own sanity prompts to detect forgetting.
  5. Online evaluation: A/B test, shadow traffic, human review of samples, track failures after launch.

Note that perplexity and training loss measure how well the model predicts text, not whether it solves your task.

# Minimal accuracy eval for a classifier model served by Ollama.
import json, ollama
rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("test.jsonl")]
hit = 0
for r in rows:
    q, gold = r["messages"][0]["content"], r["messages"][1]["content"]
    pred = ollama.chat(model="ticket-classifier", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": q}])["message"]["content"].strip()
    hit += (pred == gold)
print(f"accuracy = {hit/len(rows):.2%}")  # prints e.g. accuracy = 91.00%; run the same loop for the baseline model
// Kotlin: the same loop; `classify(q)` wraps the HTTP call from earlier sections.
fun accuracy(rows: List<Pair<String, String>>, classify: (String) -> String): Double =
    rows.count { (q, gold) -> classify(q).trim() == gold }.toDouble() / rows.size
// println("accuracy = ${"%.2f".format(accuracy(testRows, ::classify) * 100)}%")  // prints e.g. accuracy = 91.00%
static double accuracy(java.util.List<String[]> rows, java.util.function.Function<String, String> classify) {
    long hit = rows.stream().filter(r -> classify.apply(r[0]).trim().equals(r[1])).count();
    return (double) hit / rows.size();
}
// System.out.printf("accuracy = %.2f%%%n", accuracy(testRows, this::classify) * 100); // prints e.g. 91.00%

Production pitfalls. Data leakage (test examples or near-duplicates in training data gives fake scores), tiny test sets (a 50-example test has wide error bars), metrics that do not reflect users, and judging with the same model that generated the data. Keep a regression suite and re-run it on every new base model or adapter version.

Real-world examples. OpenAI Evals, the Hugging Face lm-evaluation-harness, Ragas and Promptfoo-style tools are used to automate evaluation; teams keep golden datasets in version control and run them in CI before swapping a model.

Analogy. Evaluation is the driving test: you do not let a student pass based on how well they did on practice questions they memorized.

Common interview traps.

  • Reporting results on the validation set that you tuned hyperparameters on.
  • Using LLM-as-judge without checking it against human judgments.
  • Looking only at the average; check per-category performance and the worst failures.
  • No baseline, so a fine-tune that adds nothing over a good prompt gets shipped.

notes.title: Licensing and data privacy
notes.html:
Licensing, the simple idea. "Open" models are not all equally open. Check two licenses: the model license (what you may do with the weights) and the data license (what you may train on).

  • Permissive (for example Apache 2.0, MIT): broad commercial use. Several Qwen and Mistral releases have used Apache 2.0 (verify per model).
  • Community / custom licenses (for example the Llama and Gemma licenses): commercial use is usually allowed with conditions such as acceptable-use policies, attribution or naming rules, or user-count thresholds. Read the exact text.
  • Non-commercial (for example CC BY-NC style or research-only): cannot be used in a paid product.
  • Gated models on the Hub require accepting terms before download.
  • Derivatives: a fine-tuned or merged model usually inherits the base model's license obligations. Models trained on outputs of another vendor's API may violate that vendor's terms of service; check them.
  • Open weights is not open source: weights can be downloadable while training data and code are not.

Data privacy, the simple idea. Decide where your data goes at each step and whether it contains personal data (PII: names, emails, phone numbers, health or financial details).

  • Cloud API: your prompts and files go to a third party. Check retention, whether data is used for training (many enterprise API terms say no, but verify), region, and agreements such as a DPA (data processing agreement) or a BAA for health data in the US.
  • Local or self-hosted: data stays inside your network, which simplifies GDPR/HIPAA-style compliance but you now own security, access control and logging.
  • Fine-tuning data: models can memorize and regurgitate training examples, so do not train on secrets, raw PII or customer data without consent and a legal basis. Scrub or pseudonymize first.
  • Logs and prompts: debugging logs often hold the full prompt; mask PII and set retention limits.
  • Supply chain: download weights from trusted sources, prefer safetensors, verify hashes.
# Simple redaction before sending text to any model or writing to logs (regexes are a starting point, not a guarantee).
import re
def redact(t):
    t = re.sub(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+", "[EMAIL]", t)
    return re.sub(r"\b\d{10,}\b", "[NUMBER]", t)
print(redact("Mail a.b@x.com, card 4111111111111111"))  # prints Mail [EMAIL], card [NUMBER]
val email = Regex("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.]+")
val longNum = Regex("\\b\\d{10,}\\b")
fun redact(t: String) = t.replace(email, "[EMAIL]").replace(longNum, "[NUMBER]")
fun main() = println(redact("Mail a.b@x.com, card 4111111111111111")) // prints Mail [EMAIL], card [NUMBER]
static String redact(String t) {
    return t.replaceAll("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.]+", "[EMAIL]").replaceAll("\\b\\d{10,}\\b", "[NUMBER]");
}
// System.out.println(redact("Mail a.b@x.com, card 4111111111111111")); // prints Mail [EMAIL], card [NUMBER]

Real-world examples. Samsung restricted staff use of public chatbots after employees pasted source code into one, a widely cited privacy incident. Healthcare vendors run on-prem or sign BAAs with cloud providers. Banks keep fine-tuning data inside their own VPC. Mobile apps that run Gemini Nano or MediaPipe models on-device advertise that the data never leaves the phone.

Analogy. A model license is like a software or font license: the file is on your disk, but the paper that came with it says what you are allowed to do. Sending data to a cloud API is like handing documents to an outside contractor: you need a contract about what they may keep.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming "open weights" means free for any commercial use.
  • Believing local deployment automatically means compliant; access control, encryption and retention still apply.
  • Fine-tuning on customer data without consent or de-identification.
  • Forgetting that the license and terms of the base model flow into your tuned model.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Multimodal models read images (and PDFs) by turning them into image tokens; they cost tokens, can hallucinate, and should be validated. Audio usually goes through speech-to-text first unless a provider supports audio input directly.
  • Send images and PDFs as base64 or URL content blocks; from Android, go through your own backend and never ship API keys.
  • Vision use cases (receipts, screenshots, charts) need strict schemas, a "not visible" option, validation and human review; treat text in images as untrusted.
  • Local models (Ollama, llama.cpp, Hugging Face transformers) give privacy and control with the trade-offs of weaker models and operational burden. All expose HTTP APIs, so Kotlin and Java just call a URL.
  • Quantization shrinks memory (roughly parameters times bits over 8, plus KV cache); Q4_K_M is a common default; always test quality on your task.
  • Order of attack: prompting, then RAG, then fine-tuning. RAG fixes knowledge, fine-tuning fixes behavior.
  • LoRA/QLoRA train small adapters on a frozen (possibly 4-bit) base; training is Python (peft, trl), serving and calling can be any language.
  • Evaluate on a held-out test set against a baseline, with metrics that match the task, and guard against leakage and forgetting.
  • Check licenses (model, data, derivatives) and privacy (where data goes, PII, retention) before choosing cloud or local.

questions.promptHtml: What does "multimodal" mean for an LLM, and how does a model actually "see" an image?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know images are converted to tokens that cost money and context, not magically understood.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A normal LLM reads only text; a multimodal one also accepts other kinds of input such as images or PDFs. The image is resized, cut into small patches, and a vision encoder (a small neural network) turns each patch into a vector. Those "image tokens" are fed to the LLM next to the text tokens. So images cost tokens, take context window space, and the model can still misread small details.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A token is the small chunk of text the model counts and bills in. The context window is the maximum number of tokens per request. The vision encoder produces a list of vectors that play the same role as word tokens.

photo.jpg -> resize -> patches -> vision encoder -> image tokens --+
"What is wrong with this wiring?" -> tokenizer -> text tokens -----+--> LLM -> text answer

Anthropic documents an approximate rule of width x height / 750 tokens, with large images downscaled first (verify exact numbers in current docs). Other vendors use fixed-size tiles with a cost per tile. Consequences: a bigger image means higher cost and latency, tiny text and thin lines get lost because the model sees patches and not pixels, and the output can be hallucinated (confidently invented).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying the model looks at raw pixels directly.
  • Forgetting that images count toward the context window in long conversations.
  • Treating a vision model as a precise OCR or measuring tool.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not always send the highest resolution? → Cost and latency grow with size; send the smallest image that still shows the needed detail.
  2. Is output always text? → Mostly yes for backend work; some models also generate images or speech.
  3. How would you estimate cost for 10k images a day? → Tokens per image from the vendor rule times price per token, measured from the usage field on real calls (verify rule in docs).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "you upload a picture and the model describes it." Senior: explains patches and encoder, budgets image tokens, and plans validation because of hallucination.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat app crossed its context window after users attached six photos each; the team resized images and capped images per conversation.

questions.subtopic: Sending an image: base64 vs URL
questions.promptHtml: How do you send an image to an LLM API, and when would you use base64 versus a URL?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the first thing anyone builds with vision, and the failure modes (size limits, private URLs, media type) are practical.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The image goes inside the user message as a content block next to the text block. Base64 means the bytes are encoded as text and sent in the request, which works for any file including private ones. A URL means the provider downloads it, so it must be publicly reachable. I resize first, set the right media type, and read the API key from an environment variable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: With the Anthropic API a user message holds a list of blocks. An image block has source.type (base64 or url); base64 also needs media_type (image/jpeg, image/png, image/gif, image/webp) and data. Base64 inflates size by about a third, so request size limits hit sooner. URL mode keeps the request small but fails for localhost, intranet or signed links that expired. Put the image before the question.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import base64, anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
b64 = base64.standard_b64encode(open("receipt.jpg", "rb").read()).decode()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=500,  # verify current model ids
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "image", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "image/jpeg", "data": b64}},
        {"type": "text", "text": "Extract merchant, date and total as JSON."}]}])
print(msg.content[0].text)
// Kotlin: plain REST with the JDK HttpClient. Android must call YOUR backend, never hold the key.
val b64 = java.util.Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(java.nio.file.Files.readAllBytes(java.nio.file.Path.of("receipt.jpg")))
val body = """{"model":"claude-sonnet-5-5","max_tokens":500,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":[
 {"type":"image","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"image/jpeg","data":"$b64"}},
 {"type":"text","text":"Extract merchant, date and total as JSON."}]}]}"""
val req = java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder(java.net.URI("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"))
    .header("x-api-key", System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
    .header("anthropic-version", "2023-06-01").header("content-type", "application/json")
    .POST(java.net.http.HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
println(java.net.http.HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, java.net.http.HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body())
// Java 17: same JSON, same endpoint.
String b64 = java.util.Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(java.nio.file.Files.readAllBytes(java.nio.file.Path.of("receipt.jpg")));
String body = """
  {"model":"claude-sonnet-5-5","max_tokens":500,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":[
   {"type":"image","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"image/jpeg","data":"%s"}},
   {"type":"text","text":"Extract merchant, date and total as JSON."}]}]}""".formatted(b64);
HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages"))
    .header("x-api-key", System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
    .header("anthropic-version", "2023-06-01").header("content-type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
System.out.println(HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrong media_type (says jpeg, bytes are png).
  • URL that needs a login or points to localhost.
  • Sending a 12 MB camera photo as base64 without resizing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the answer sit in the response? → In content[0].text.
  2. Why not call the API straight from Android? → The key would ship in the APK; call your own backend.
  3. Why might the same image cost differently across vendors? → Different resize and tiling rules per vendor.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "base64 it and post." Senior: picks base64 vs URL by privacy and size, resizes, validates media type, and routes mobile traffic through a backend.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An internal tool used signed S3 URLs that expired in 5 minutes; queued jobs failed with fetch errors until the team switched to base64.

questions.promptHtml: How can an LLM read a PDF, and why is sending a 300-page PDF on every request a bad idea?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Document Q&A is the most common multimodal feature, and cost blow-ups are common.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Many APIs accept a PDF as a document block. The provider extracts the text and also renders each page as an image, so the model can read tables, charts and scans. Every page costs tokens, so a long PDF repeated on every request is slow and expensive. For repeated questions I use prompt caching (cheap reuse of an identical prefix) or RAG (search first, send only the relevant pieces).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The block looks like {"type":"document","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"application/pdf","data":...}}. Page and size limits exist (verify in current docs). Scanned PDFs have no text layer, so the page images do the work and accuracy needs checking.

small PDF, one question      -> document block directly
big PDF, many questions      -> prompt cache the PDF prefix, or RAG
many PDFs                    -> RAG over a vector index

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import base64
pdf = base64.standard_b64encode(open("contract.pdf", "rb").read()).decode()
content = [{"type": "document", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": pdf}},
           {"type": "text", "text": "List the termination clauses with page numbers."}]
# pass `content` as the user message content in client.messages.create(...)
val pdfB64 = java.util.Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(java.nio.file.Files.readAllBytes(java.nio.file.Path.of("contract.pdf")))
val content = """[{"type":"document","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"application/pdf","data":"$pdfB64"}},
 {"type":"text","text":"List the termination clauses with page numbers."}]"""
// put `content` into messages[0].content of the same POST as the image example
String pdfB64 = java.util.Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(java.nio.file.Files.readAllBytes(java.nio.file.Path.of("contract.pdf")));
String content = """
  [{"type":"document","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"application/pdf","data":"%s"}},
   {"type":"text","text":"List the termination clauses with page numbers."}]""".formatted(pdfB64);
// put `content` into messages[0].content of the same POST as the image example

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Re-sending the whole PDF for each follow-up question.
  • Assuming a scanned PDF has extractable text.
  • Ignoring page and size limits.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When RAG instead of caching? → When the corpus is large or changes, or the answer needs only a few passages.
  2. How do you get page numbers? → Ask for them, or keep page metadata in your chunks.
  3. Is the answer guaranteed correct? → No; ask for quotes and verify.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "attach the PDF." Senior: estimates tokens per page, picks caching vs RAG by question volume, and adds citation checks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A legal tool resent a 200-page contract per question and its monthly bill tripled; caching the prefix cut it sharply.

questions.promptHtml: Why would a team run an LLM locally, what is Ollama, and how does your Kotlin or Java code call it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can weigh privacy and cost against quality and operations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A local model runs on your own machine instead of a vendor cloud. The weights (the big file of numbers) load into RAM or GPU memory (VRAM). Reasons: data privacy, no per-token bill, offline use, version control. The cost: smaller models are usually weaker than frontier ones and you own operations. Ollama downloads models and serves them over HTTP at http://localhost:11434, so any language just makes an HTTP call.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Ollama builds on llama.cpp and runs quantized GGUF models. It has its own /api/chat endpoint and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint at /v1, so code written for the OpenAI client often needs only a new base URL. Local is not automatically cheaper: an idle GPU and engineer time cost more than API calls at low volume. Ollama has no authentication by default, so never expose the port to the internet.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import ollama  # pip install ollama ; run `ollama pull llama3.2` first
r = ollama.chat(model="llama3.2", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain quantization in one line."}])
print(r["message"]["content"])
val body = """{"model":"llama3.2","stream":false,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain quantization in one line."}]}"""
val req = java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder(java.net.URI("http://localhost:11434/api/chat"))
    .POST(java.net.http.HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
println(java.net.http.HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, java.net.http.HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body())
String body = """
  {"model":"llama3.2","stream":false,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain quantization in one line."}]}""";
HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://localhost:11434/api/chat"))
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
System.out.println(HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming local is always cheaper.
  • Exposing port 11434 publicly.
  • Expecting laptop-sized models to match frontier reasoning.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Spring AI or LangChain4j with Ollama? → Both have Ollama integrations; swap cloud and local by configuration (verify property names).
  2. Vision locally? → Use a vision-capable model and pass images in the message.
  3. Dev vs prod? → Many teams use Ollama locally and in CI, then a hosted or vLLM-served model in production.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "free, runs offline." Senior: counts utilization, quality gap, ops burden and security of the endpoint.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team used Ollama in CI to avoid API spend and caught prompt regressions before release.

questions.promptHtml: What is quantization, and roughly how much memory does an 8B model need at 16-bit versus 4-bit?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Sizing hardware is a daily local-model task, and the arithmetic is quick to check.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Quantization stores each model weight with fewer bits, such as 8 or 4 instead of 16, so the model is smaller and often faster at a small quality cost. Memory is about parameters times bits divided by 8, plus overhead. An 8B model is about 16 GB at 16-bit, about 8 GB at 8-bit and about 4.5 to 5 GB at 4-bit, plus the KV cache.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Weights are grouped in blocks; each block stores a scale plus low-bit integers, converted back approximately at compute time. 8B x 16 bits / 8 = 16 GB; 8B x 4 / 8 = 4 GB, and real files run slightly bigger because of scales. The KV cache (stored attention keys and values for tokens so far) grows with context length and needs extra GB. Decoding is mostly memory-bandwidth-bound, so fewer bytes per token usually means faster generation. 8-bit is nearly lossless; 4-bit loses a little, visible in math, code and non-English; smaller models suffer more.

Model 16-bit 8-bit 4-bit
8B ~16 GB ~8 GB ~4.5-5 GB
70B ~140 GB ~70 GB ~40 GB

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the KV cache and runtime overhead.
  • Mixing up quantization with pruning or distillation.
  • Judging quality only by perplexity instead of your own task.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a 70B 4-bit model run on a 24 GB GPU? → No, about 40 GB is needed; offload to CPU RAM or use a smaller model.
  2. Does quantization speed up training? → Not directly; QLoRA only keeps the frozen base in 4-bit.
  3. How do you verify quality? → Run quantized and original on your own evaluation set.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "smaller model, a bit worse." Senior: does the byte arithmetic, includes KV cache, and measures task quality.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 13B model at 4-bit fit in VRAM at 2k context but ran out of memory at 16k because the KV cache grew.

questions.promptHtml: When do you use prompting, RAG or fine-tuning, and in what order do you try them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common GenAI architecture question; wrong answers waste months.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Prompting means better instructions and examples; RAG fetches relevant facts from your documents at question time; fine-tuning continues training so the model's behavior changes. RAG fixes missing or changing knowledge; fine-tuning fixes style, format or a narrow skill. I try prompting first, then RAG, then fine-tuning, and I measure a baseline before each step.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Missing or changing facts?            -> RAG
Style/format/narrow skill, prompts    -> fine-tune
  tried and still failing or too long
Unclear instructions?                 -> improve the prompt
Prompting RAG Fine-tuning
Fixes instructions, format knowledge behavior
Update facts edit prompt re-index retrain
Citations no possible no

Fine-tuning does not reliably add facts, and its knowledge is frozen at training time. It pays off when a small cheap model must match a big one on one task, or very long repeated prompts should be removed.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def first_try(fresh_facts, style_or_format, prompt_tuned):
    if fresh_facts: return "RAG"
    if style_or_format and prompt_tuned: return "fine-tune"
    return "prompting"
fun firstTry(fresh: Boolean, style: Boolean, tuned: Boolean) = when {
    fresh -> "RAG"
    style && tuned -> "fine-tune"
    else -> "prompting"
}
static String firstTry(boolean fresh, boolean style, boolean tuned) {
    if (fresh) return "RAG";
    if (style && tuned) return "fine-tune";
    return "prompting";
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Fine-tune on our documents so it knows them" (usually a RAG job).
  • Fine-tuning without a baseline.
  • Forgetting re-tuning on every base-model upgrade.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you combine them? → Yes: RAG for facts plus a tuned model for tone or format.
  2. Minimum data for fine-tuning? → A few hundred clean examples at least; quality beats quantity.
  3. Why do citations favor RAG? → Retrieved passages can be shown; weights cannot.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "fine-tune for domain knowledge." Senior: separates knowledge from behavior, orders by cost and reversibility, and insists on an evaluation set first.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A support bot fine-tuned on help articles gave outdated answers within weeks; moving to RAG fixed freshness.

questions.promptHtml: Is "open weights" the same as free for any commercial use? What do you check before using a model in a product?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: License mistakes surface late and legally.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. Open weights only means you can download the file. I read the model license: permissive ones such as Apache 2.0 or MIT allow broad commercial use; community licenses (Llama, Gemma) usually allow it with conditions like acceptable-use rules or user-count thresholds; non-commercial licenses forbid paid products. A fine-tuned or merged model normally inherits the base license, and training on another vendor's outputs may breach that vendor's terms.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Two licenses matter: the model license (weights) and the data license (what you train on). Gated models on Hugging Face need accepted terms before download. Open weights is not open source: training data and code may be closed. Always check the exact text per model version (verify), because licenses differ even inside one family. Keep a record of model, version and license in your repo.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming Hugging Face availability means commercial use is allowed.
  • Forgetting that derivatives inherit obligations.
  • Ignoring terms of service when generating training data with an API model.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where is the license? → The model card and license file on the Hub.
  2. User-count thresholds? → Some community licenses require a special agreement above a user limit; read the text.
  3. Who decides? → Legal, with engineering supplying the facts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "it's open source." Senior: checks model and data licenses, derivatives, ToS of synthetic data sources, and records them.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A startup found a non-commercial licence on its chosen model a week before launch and had to switch.

questions.promptHtml: A model API does not accept raw audio. How do you build a voice or meeting feature on top of it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of the ASR, LLM, TTS pipeline and its practical details.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use speech-to-text first. ASR (automatic speech recognition) turns audio into text, for example Whisper, a hosted transcription API, or Android SpeechRecognizer. The text goes to the LLM, and optionally a text-to-speech step speaks the reply. For long recordings I chunk the audio, keep timestamps for citations, and add diarization (speaker labels) as a separate step if needed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
audio -> ASR -> text (+ timestamps) -> LLM -> text -> TTS (optional)

Some providers (Gemini, GPT audio models) accept audio directly, and end-to-end speech models cut latency, but support varies (verify current docs). Pipelines add latency per stage, so stream partial results. Audio holds personal data, so check where it is processed. Whisper can run locally.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import whisper  # pip install openai-whisper
text = whisper.load_model("base").transcribe("meeting.mp3")["text"]
print(text[:200])  # then send `text` to the LLM
// Android: SpeechRecognizer.createSpeechRecognizer(context) streams partial text (verify API in Android docs).
// JVM backend: multipart POST the file to a Whisper service, read {"text": "..."}.
// No first-party Whisper binding on the JVM: POST audio to a Python Whisper service or hosted
// transcription API, read the text field, then use it as a normal prompt.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming every model accepts audio.
  • Sending a 2-hour recording in one piece.
  • Losing timestamps and speakers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you cut latency for voice chat? → Stream ASR partials, stream the LLM, start TTS on the first sentence.
  2. Long meeting summary? → Chunk transcript, summarize chunks, then summarize summaries.
  3. Privacy? → Prefer local Whisper or a provider with a data-processing agreement.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "transcribe then prompt." Senior: designs chunking, diarization, streaming and privacy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A call-center QA tool lost speaker identity, so the LLM blamed customers for agent errors until diarization was added.

questions.promptHtml: Compare llama.cpp, Hugging Face transformers and a server like vLLM. Which would you pick for a laptop demo, for fine-tuning, and for production serving?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you know the local-model ecosystem and its limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: llama.cpp is a C/C++ engine that runs quantized GGUF models well on CPUs and consumer GPUs and offers an OpenAI-compatible llama-server. Hugging Face transformers is the Python library for loading, training and experimenting with almost any model. vLLM is a GPU serving engine with continuous batching and PagedAttention for high throughput. Laptop demo: Ollama or llama.cpp. Fine-tuning: transformers with peft/trl. Production on GPUs: vLLM.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Ollama wraps llama.cpp. GGUF is an inference format and is not used for training. Hugging Face models are usually in safetensors; avoid pickle-based .bin files from unknown sources, since pickle can run code on load. Apply the chat template (apply_chat_template) or an instruct model degrades. Using plain transformers for many concurrent users wastes the GPU because it lacks continuous batching.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from openai import OpenAI
c = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8080/v1", api_key="not-needed")  # llama-server or vLLM
print(c.chat.completions.create(model="local", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}]).choices[0].message.content)
val body = """{"model":"local","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hi"}]}"""
val req = java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder(java.net.URI("http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions"))
    .header("content-type", "application/json")
    .POST(java.net.http.HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
// answer at choices[0].message.content
// LangChain4j can target any OpenAI-compatible server by base URL (verify builder names in its docs):
// OpenAiChatModel.builder().baseUrl("http://localhost:8080/v1").apiKey("not-needed").modelName("local").build()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Loading unknown pickle checkpoints.
  • Forgetting the chat template.
  • Thinking GGUF can be used to train.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is continuous batching? → New requests join a running batch each step, keeping the GPU busy.
  2. Why is the OpenAI-compatible API useful? → Clients stay unchanged when the backend switches.
  3. Context setting? → Set -c explicitly; defaults can be small.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Ollama is easiest." Senior: matches the engine to workload (edge, training, throughput) and knows format and security issues.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A prototype served via plain transformers fell over at 20 concurrent users; moving to a batching server multiplied throughput.

questions.contextHtml: An expense app extracts merchant, date and total from receipt photos with a vision model, 40,000 receipts a day. Finance finds that about 2 percent (800 a day) have a total that does not appear on the receipt, usually on blurry or cropped photos. The JSON always parses. Phone photos are 4000 by 3000 px and are downscaled by the app to 800 px wide before upload. The prompt says "Return JSON with merchant, date, total."
questions.promptHtml: How do you diagnose and fix wrong totals that look perfectly valid?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a bigger model" or "ask it to be more accurate." That ignores that the format is valid, the input is degraded, and the prompt gives the model no way to say it cannot see the value.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which photo conditions correlate with errors (blur, crop, glare)? Is the total missing from the image or misread? What does a wrong total cost the business? Is there a human review step?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route receipts failing checks (below) to a human review queue so bad totals stop reaching finance.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 800 px downscale destroys small digits; (b) prompt has no "not visible" escape so the model guesses; (c) cropped receipts hide the total; (d) model hallucination under blur.
  4. How I'd verify each: Take 200 failing samples, compare at 800 px vs 1600 px; re-run with a null-if-unsure prompt; check usage for image token counts; look at crop rates.
  5. Root cause: Low resolution plus a prompt that forces an answer made the model invent plausible numbers.
  6. Fix: Raise upload resolution (crop to the receipt and auto-rotate on device), prompt "use null if not clearly visible, do not guess", and validate in code: line items must sum to the total, total must be a positive number.
  7. Prevention: Schema validation, a labeled test set of 500 receipts with per-field accuracy in CI, and tracking the null rate and review rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Higher resolution costs more image tokens (measure per receipt); I would not trust model confidence text; I would not auto-approve large totals.
import json
def check(raw):
    d = json.loads(raw)
    t = d.get("total")
    if t is None: return "review"
    items = d.get("items") or []
    if items and abs(sum(i["price"] for i in items) - t) > 0.01: return "review"
    return "ok"
fun check(total: Double?, items: List<Double>): String = when {
    total == null -> "review"
    items.isNotEmpty() && kotlin.math.abs(items.sum() - total) > 0.01 -> "review"
    else -> "ok"
}
static String check(Double total, java.util.List<Double> items) {
    if (total == null) return "review";
    double sum = items.stream().mapToDouble(Double::doubleValue).sum();
    return (!items.isEmpty() && Math.abs(sum - total) > 0.01) ? "review" : "ok";
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cost doubles after raising resolution → crop to the receipt region first and only upscale when a cheap first pass returns null.
  • Fraudulent edited receipts → separate fraud checks; the extractor is not a forensic tool.
  • Same bug but handwritten receipts → lower expectations and a larger review share.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team celebrated 99 percent valid JSON for weeks while a silent 2 percent of totals were guesses; adding a sum check found them in a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the model and asks for "more accurate" output.
  • Hire: identifies resolution and the missing null option, adds validation.
  • Strong hire: adds labeled eval set, review routing, cost trade-off and monitoring of null and review rates.

questions.promptHtml: You see model files named Q8_0, Q5_K_M and Q4_K_M. How do you choose one, and how do you size the GPU for it including context?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical hardware planning, not just definitions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Those are GGUF quantization levels: the number is roughly the bits per weight, so lower is smaller and lossier. Q8_0 is nearly lossless, Q5_K_M is a good middle, Q4_K_M is the popular default balance. I estimate memory as parameters times bits / 8, add several GB for the KV cache that grows with context length, and then test the candidate on my own task before choosing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Example: 8B at about 4.8 bits per weight is ~4.8 GB. At 8k context the KV cache may add around 1 GB or more depending on the architecture (verify for your model), so a 6 GB GPU is tight. Other formats: GPTQ and AWQ are GPU-oriented 4-bit post-training quantization (used with vLLM and transformers); bitsandbytes NF4 loads 4-bit inside transformers and underlies QLoRA. Start from the largest quantization that fits comfortably and step down only if latency or memory requires it, comparing task metrics each time.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
